# Why Markdown?

## What is Markdown (.md)?

- A way of writing text and styling text that can be read with or without a markdown editor.
- A lightweight alternative to HTML.
- Probably the foremost standard for documentation in scientific computing.

## Different ".md"

- Markdown is a fairly open standard, and not all Markdown is exactly the same, but tends to follow common rules.
- I will teach GitHub Markdown, a major but not the only standard.
- These slides are generated in Quarto Markdown, an extension of the standard.
- [Dillinger](https://dillinger.io/) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md/) are popular Markdown platforms.

## What is the relation to GitHub?

- By convention, every GitHub repository should come with a README.md file.
- By default, GitHub will style this and display it on the main repository page.
- This is how you should communicate to anyone who discovers your code or is looking for your code *what the code does*.

## Conceptualizing

- Suppose you are describing some code, like `tax.py` 
	- You may wish to link to primary source documents on tax policy.
	- You may wish to create paragraphs, unnumbered and numbered lists.
	- You may wish to embed images, code snippets.
	- You may wish to use rich **bold** or *italic* text.

## Problem Solving

- Markdown
  	- Uses existing, common typographical characters
	- Corresponds to widely standardized HTML
	- Is human-readable without being rendered in HTML
- Can be:
  	- Written in any text editor.
	- Authored in a dedicated Markdown editor.

## Stepping Back

- `git` was made to solve this exact problem!
- The world leading scientific computing operating system, Linux, was being developed remotely via volunteers.
- They used millions of lines of code in complex file structures.
- They had to have a way to keep track of everything!

## We will

- Introduce Markdown syntax:
	- Style text
	- Link to resources
- Use "Markdown" to:
	- Document our code with Markdown
	  
## Documentation

- Previously, we learned about comments.
  	- Lines in code that do not affect what the code does, but help human users understand it.
- Often we document repositories with README files.
  	- *Often* as `README.md`, a "Markdown" file.
- We introduce Markdown.

# Text

## A note

- These slides are written in Markdown.
- I'll show the Markdown in a left column and how it is rendered. on the right.
- If you wish to follow along, the most obvious way is <https://dillinger.io/>

## Text

- The most natural thing to do in a `README.md` is simply write text.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
Unremarkable text.
```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Unremakrable text.

:::

::::

## Bold

- Enclose text in double `**`, double `__` or HTML style `<b>` to bold text.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
We can make text **bold**.

We can make text __bold__.

We can make text <b>bold</b>.
```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

We can make text **bold**.

We can make text __bold__.

We can make text <b>bold</b>.

:::

::::

## Italic

- Enclose text in single `*`, single `_` or HTML style `<i>` to italicize text.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
We can make text *italic*.

We can make text _italic_.

We can make text <i>italic</i>.
```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

We can make text *italic*.

We can make text _italic_.

We can make text <i>italic</i>.

:::

::::

## Strikethrough

- Very helpful to show what not to do.
  
:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
We can make text ~strikethrough~ sometimes.

We can make text ~~strikethrough~~.

We can make text <s>strikethrough</s>.

```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

We can make text ~strikethrough~ sometimes.

We can make text ~~strikethrough~~.

We can make text <s>strikethrough</s>.

:::

::::

## Nesting

- As a rule, formatting can be nested but not overlapped.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
__Bold__, *italic*, or ***both***.

__Bold, *nested,*__ or *italic*.

__Can't be *overlapped__, however*.

```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

__Bold__, *italic*, or ***both***.

__Bold, *nested,*__ or *italic*.

__Can't be *overlapped__, however*.
:::

::::

## Sub/superscript

- In scientific publication, we often require subscripts and superscripts.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
Squaring *x* as *x*<sup>2</sup> or *x*^2^

Denoting a Helium-3 isotope as He<sub>3</sub> or He~3~.

```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Squaring *x* as *x*<sup>2</sup> or x^2^

Denoting a Helium-3 isotope as He<sub>3</sub> or He~3~.

:::

::::


## When .md fails

- A number of of formatting options require the heavier-weight HTML tags.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
Underlining is <u>rarely</u> used.

Some editors support ==.md== or <mark>HTML</mark> highlighting.
```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Underlining is <u>rarely</u> used.

Some editors support ==.md== or <mark>HTML</mark> highlighting.

:::

::::

# Quotes

## Blockquotes

- Quotes are used frequently in Markdown, for various reasons.
- When quoting another writer, or a source, often use blockquotes:

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
> Veni, vidi, vici.

<blockquote>Oṃ maṇi padme hūm̐</blockquote>


```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

> Veni, vidi, vici.

<blockquote>Oṃ maṇi padme hūm̐</blockquote>
:::

::::

## Unicode

- We note Markdown generally supports unicode characters as well as anything else does - usually exactly as well as your browser.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
> ॐ मणि पद्मे हूँ
```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

> ॐ मणि पद्मे हूँ
:::

::::


## Backticks

- The backtick character `` ` `` (near `~`) has special meaning in Markdown.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

````{.md}
Single back for `print('hi')`

Use triple backtick for:

```
for i in range(10):
	print(i*i)
```

````

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Single back for `print('hi')`

Use triple backtick for:

```
for i in range(10):
	print(i*i)
```

:::

::::

## Syntax Highlighting

- Often we want codeblocks to have highlighting as we see in a code editor.
- Specify the file extension immediately after the opening triple backtick.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

````{.md}
```py
def ten_sqs():
	for i in range(10):
		print(i*i)
	return
```

````

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```py
def ten_sqs():
	for i in range(10):
		print(i*i)
	return
```

:::

::::

- In Quarto Markdown, this also changes background (this is non-standard).

# Lists

## Better than sentences

- As a rule, it's a good idea to break text up.
- Note that `*` or `-` work and linebreaks don't break the list.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
- Use lists.
- Be concise.

* Use bullets.
* Save space.
```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

- Use lists.
- Be concise.

* Use bullets.
* Save space.
:::

::::

## Nesting

- Lists can be nested via indentiation with whitespace.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
- Lists are great!
  - Easy to read.
    - Either as markdown or text!
  - Easy to type.
- Try them out! 
```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

- Lists are great!
  - Easy to read.
    - Either as markdown or text!
  - Easy to type.
- Try them out!

:::

::::

## Numbering

- Lists are numbered automatically.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="30%"}

```{.md}
1. One
1. Two
1. Three
1. Four
   1. Four and half
1. Five
```

- There is no graceful way to start a list at zero.

:::


::: {.column width="20%"}

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

1. One
1. Two
1. Three
1. Four
   1. Four and half
1. Five

:::

::::

## Task lists

- You can also make "task lists".
- Try clicking those boxes!


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
- [x] Open the door
- [ ] Get on the floor
- [ ] Walk the dinosaur
```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

- [x] Open the door
- [ ] Get on the floor
- [ ] Walk the dinosaur

:::

::::

# Lines

## Line breaks

- There's a few ways to perform a .md line break.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
Two spaces 
break lines  
one space 
does not.
```


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Two spaces 
break lines  
one space 
does not.

:::

::::

## Line breaks

- Invisible line breaks are very annoying and `\` is often preferred. 

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
Back slash\
breaks lines
just like  
two spaces.
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Back slash\
breaks lines.
just like  
two spaces.

:::

::::

## Line breaks

- These work inside lists. 

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
- Some items\
  are long.
- Some aren't.
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

- Some items\
  are long.
- Some aren't.

:::

::::

## HTML

- The HTML `<br/>` will often works as well.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
Even in the middle<br/>of lines.
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Even in the middle<br/>of lines.

:::

::::

# Links

## URL links

- As a rule, you can link anywhere on the internet.
- Place the link text in `[]` and the URL in `()`

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
[Read more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markdown)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

[Read more](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markdown)

:::

::::

## Images

- Use `![]` before a link to an image file, like a `.png`, `.jpg`, or `.svg`.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cd-public/scicom/refs/heads/main/qmd/src/julia.png)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cd-public/scicom/refs/heads/main/qmd/src/julia.png)

:::

::::

## Relative Links

- Within a GitHub markdown document, you can also link to images within the repository.
- This `.md` document is in `/main/qmd/src/` so I can just use:

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
![](julia.png)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](julia.png)

:::

::::

## Footnotes

- Generally, by the time you are using footnotes you should switch to a different platform (LaTeX).
- But they exist!

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
Use numbered[^1] or named[^footnote] notes.

[^1]: I'm number one!
	[^footnote]: I'm a footnote!
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Use numbered[^1] or named[^footnote] notes.

[^1]: I'm number one!
[^footnote]: I'm a footnote!

:::

::::

# Sections

## Headings

- In my markdown, headings correspond to slides or sections.
- They are `#` prefixed and get their own line.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
# Heading
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

<h1>Heading</h1>

:::

::::

## Subheadings

- In my markdown, headings correspond to slides or sections.
- They are `#` prefixed and get their own line.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
## Subheadings

### Get

#### Progressively

##### Smaller
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

<h2>Subheadings</h2>

<h3>Get</h3>

<h4>Progressively</h4>

<h5>Smaller</h5>

:::

::::

## Links

- We can link to sections using all lowercase (and replace spaces with `-`)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
The previous heading was [Links](#links) part of the notes.
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


The previous heading was [Links](#links) part of the notes.


:::

::::

# Callouts

## Optional Features

- Some editors support callout blocks.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{.md}
> [!NOTE]
> GitHub note.

::: {.callout-note}
Quarto note.
:::

> 📝 **Note:** Blockquote/emoji hack.
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


> [!NOTE]
> GitHub note (doesn't work here).

::: {.callout-note}
Quarto note.
:::

> 📝 **Note:** Blockquote/emoji hack.


:::

::::
